title: The US electrical grid from power plant to wall outlet
summary: A map-style tour of the US grid: regions and interconnections down to a house panel — geography first, not a single causal essay.

blocks.title: Read the grid like a map
blocks.body: This sibling page (-b) treats the path from power plant to wall outlet as nested geography: interconnection → region → utility territory → substation neighborhood → house. It is deliberately not a pure causal chain of "then the voltage becomes…" — zoom levels are the spine.

blocks.title: Sibling artifact exists
blocks.body: Instinct's gn-the-us-electrical-grid-from-power-plant-to-wall-outlet (no -b) covers stage-by-stage causality. This -b file is the map metaphor. Do not merge them mentally into one page.

blocks.heading: Why interconnections matter on a map
blocks.body: Inside one interconnection, machines stay in lockstep frequency. Between interconnections, power moves only through special ties (or not at all). If you only remember one map fact: your outlet's frequency story is regional, not "national" in the synchronous sense.

blocks.heading: Who colors your county
blocks.body: Investor-owned utilities, municipal utilities, and cooperatives paint different territories on the same state map. The outlet in your wall sits in someone's service territory — that someone maintains the poles, the meters, and the outage map you refresh during storms.

blocks.caption: Overlapping polygons are normal. Grid maps are layered stickers, not one crayon.

blocks.heading: Find your substation on a mental map
items: Transmission lines arrive at a fenced yard with transformers and buswork.
Voltage steps down to distribution levels used on street poles or underground feeders.
Feeders leave like spokes — each feeder is a neighborhood-scale branch.
Faults and switching on one feeder can reconfigure who is lit without changing the interconnection map.

blocks.heading: How to use -b versus the causal sibling
blocks.body: Use this page when you need to orient: where am I on the national map, whose territory, which substation neighborhood. Use the non -b sibling when you need the physics story of conversion stages. Together they are a pair; separately they keep map and mechanism from smudging.

blocks.body: When a breaker trips, remember which map layer failed — branch circuit, feeder, or something bigger on the outage map.
